questions.passage: Linguists rarely have the opportunity to observe a language being born, but the founding of a school for deaf children on the island of Merrow in 1986 provided exactly such a case. Before the school opened, most deaf islanders lived in isolation from one another and communicated with their hearing families through simple, home-made gestures. Once brought together, the first pupils rapidly developed a shared system of signs. This early system, researchers found, was effective but loosely organised: signers varied in how they ordered words and rarely marked who did what to whom. The decisive changes came with the next generation of children, who entered the school at the age of four or five and learned the system from older pupils rather than inventing it. These younger signers did not simply copy what they saw. They regularised it, introducing consistent ways of indicating space, time and grammatical roles that the older signers seldom used, even though the latter had been signing for longer. For many researchers, the Merrow case supports the view that young children are not merely passive learners of the language around them but active contributors to its structure. Others are more cautious, noting that the school also brought increased contact with written language and with visiting teachers, influences that may have shaped the language in ways that are difficult to separate from the children's own contribution.
questions.text: According to the passage, before the school was founded, deaf people on Merrow ----.
options: had already developed a highly structured sign language that was used throughout the island
lacked a common sign language and used gestures developed within their own families
were taught to communicate through written language
attended schools on the mainland
learned sign language from visiting teachers
questions.explanation: Okul açılmadan önce sağır adalıların birbirinden yalıtılmış yaşadığı ve aileleriyle evde geliştirilmiş basit jestlerle iletişim kurduğu belirtilir: 'lacked a common sign language and used gestures developed within their own families'. 'Had already developed a highly structured sign language' parçayla çelişir; yazı diliyle ve ziyaretçi öğretmenlerle temas okulla birlikte başlamıştır.

For many researchers, the Merrow case supports the view that young children are not merely passive learners of the language around them but active contributors to its structure. Others are more cautious, noting that the school also brought increased contact with written language and with visiting teachers, influences that may have shaped the language in ways that are difficult to separate from the children's own contribution.

questions.passage: Linguists rarely have the opportunity to observe a language being born, but the founding of a school for deaf children on the island of Merrow in 1986 provided exactly such a case. Before the school opened, most deaf islanders lived in isolation from one another and communicated with their hearing families through simple, home-made gestures. Once brought together, the first pupils rapidly developed a shared system of signs. This early system, researchers found, was effective but loosely organised: signers varied in how they ordered words and rarely marked who did what to whom. The decisive changes came with the next generation of children, who entered the school at the age of four or five and learned the system from older pupils rather than inventing it. These younger signers did not simply copy what they saw. They regularised it, introducing consistent ways of indicating space, time and grammatical roles that the older signers seldom used, even though the latter had been signing for longer. For many researchers, the Merrow case supports the view that young children are not merely passive learners of the language around them but active contributors to its structure. Others are more cautious, noting that the school also brought increased contact with written language and with visiting teachers, influences that may have shaped the language in ways that are difficult to separate from the children's own contribution.
questions.text: The researchers described as 'more cautious' suggest that ----.
options: the second generation did not actually change the language
the Merrow case shows that adults learn languages better than children
factors other than children's own creativity may have contributed to the development of the language
visiting teachers deliberately prevented the language from developing
written language had no influence on the signers
questions.explanation: Temkinli araştırmacılar, yazı diliyle ve ziyaretçi öğretmenlerle artan temasın dili çocukların katkısından ayırt edilmesi güç biçimlerde etkilemiş olabileceğini söyler: 'factors other than children's own creativity may have contributed to the development of the language'. 'Written language had no influence on the signers' bunun tam tersidir; öğretmenlerin gelişimi kasten engellediği de söylenmez.
